text: Preface This report, using analyses of recently available census and survey data on the population of China, presents the demographic history of China during the past 30 years.
text_raw:
Preface
This report, using analyses of recently available census and survey data on
the population of China, presents the demographic history of China during the
past 30 years.

text: The report uses detailed assessments of data from a major 1982 fertility survey and the 1982 census of China, which became available at the end of 1983, to develop estimates of three major population processes for 1952-82: fertility, nuptiality, and mortality.
text_raw:
The report uses detailed assessments of data from a major 1982
fertility survey and the 1982 census of China, which became available at the
end of 1983, to develop estimates of three major population processes for
1952-82: fertility, nuptiality, and mortality.

text: With the rapid expansion in world population in recent decades, fertility and its determinants have been urgent topics for research.
text_raw:
With the rapid expansion in world population in recent decades, fertility
and its determinants have been urgent topics for research.

text: Attempts to affect population growth have focused on reducing fertility, with some apparent effect.
text_raw:
Attempts to affect
population growth have focused on reducing fertility, with some apparent
effect.

text: The peak rate of growth in the world's population has now passed although growth is still at a high level in almost all the developing countries.
text_raw:
The peak rate of growth in the world's population has now passed
although growth is still at a high level in almost all the developing countries.

text: In absolute numbers, the increase in the world's population continues to rise: according to United Nations medium projections, more people will be added each year for the next 35-40 years than were added in 1980.
text_raw:
In
absolute numbers, the increase in the world's population continues to rise:
according to United Nations medium projections, more people will be added
each year for the next 35-40 years than were added in 1980.

text: In this context, China's recent rapid declines in fertility and mortality are remarkable; moreover, China's decline in fertility has contributed substantially to the modest reduction in the world rate of population growth.
text_raw:
In this context,
China's recent rapid declines in fertility and mortality are remarkable;
moreover, China's decline in fertility has contributed substantially to the modest
reduction in the world rate of population growth.

text: This report on China is number 27 in a series of reports prepared by the Committee on Population and Demography and its several panels.
text_raw:
This report on China is number 27 in a series of reports prepared by the
Committee on Population and Demography and its several panels.

text: Summary In 1982 the People's Republic of China carried out a census with a more comprehensive interview schedule than ever before employed in China and using a very large, carefully chosen, and extensively trained field staff.
text_raw:
Summary
In 1982 the People's Republic of China carried out a census with a more
comprehensive interview schedule than ever before employed in China and
using a very large, carefully chosen, and extensively trained field staff.

text: The census was preceded by pilot surveys to test the instruments and field procedures.
text_raw:
The
census was preceded by pilot surveys to test the instruments and field
procedures.

text: A tabulation of 10 percent of the individual returns has been completed, published in China, and made available abroad in limited circulation.
text_raw:
A tabulation of 10 percent of the individual returns has been
completed, published in China, and made available abroad in limited
circulation.

text: Also in 1982 a fertility survey covering a very large sample of households (total population of more than 1 million) was conducted in China, and its results have been published in great detail in a special issue of the Chinese Journal Population and Economics.
text_raw:
Also in 1982 a fertility survey covering a very large sample of
households (total population of more than 1 million) was conducted in China,
and its results have been published in great detail in a special issue of the
Chinese Journal 
Population and Economics.

text: In addition, the distribution of the population by sex and single years of age as enumerated in the censuses of 1953 and 1964 has been recently released.
text_raw:
In addition, the distribution of the
population by sex and single years of age as enumerated in the censuses of 1953
and 1964 has been recently released.

text: This new information, supplemented by time series of registered births and deaths and end-of-year population totals extending back to the 1950s and by data from other large recent surveys, provides a sound basis for constructing an accurate and detailed history of the remarkable changes in fertility, mortality, and marriage that have occurred in China since the People's Republic was established.
text_raw:
This new information, supplemented by
time series of registered births and deaths and end-of-year population totals
extending back to the 1950s and by data from other large recent surveys,
provides a sound basis for constructing an accurate and detailed history of the
remarkable changes in fertility, mortality, and marriage that have occurred in
China since the People's Republic was established.

text_raw:

and childbearing of women up to age 67 in the 1/1,000 fertility survey of 1982.

1981.

text: Fertility Rates.
text_raw: Fertility Rates.

text: The birth rate in China has been higher than that listed in official sources.
text_raw:
The birth rate in China has been higher than that listed in
official sources.

text: In the 1950s the birth rate was generally above 40 per 1,000 until a precipitous fallâ€”from 42.5 per 1,000 in 1957 to 21.9 in 1961â€”that coincided with the Great Leap Forward and the ensuing years of economic disruption and famine.
text_raw:
In the 1950s the birth rate was generally above 40 per 1,000
until a precipitous fallâ€”from 42.5 per 1,000 in 1957 to 21.9 in 1961â€”that
coincided with the Great Leap Forward and the ensuing years of economic
disruption and famine.

text: The post-crisis peak birth rate in 1963 was just short of 50 births per 1,000.
text_raw:
The post-crisis peak birth rate in 1963 was just short of
50 births per 1,000.

text: A more useful fertility measure, the total fertility rate (TFR)â€”the average number of children that would be born in a lifetime to women subject to the birth rates by age in a given periodâ€”was about 6.0 before the Great Leap Forward, declined to 3.3 in 1961, rose to 7.5 in 1963, returned to 6.0 in the mid-1960s, fell steeply to only 2.2 in 1980, and then rose slightly to over 2.6 in 1981 and 1982.
text_raw:
A more useful fertility measure, the total fertility rate (TFR)â€”the average
number of children that would be born in a lifetime to women subject to the
birth rates by age in a given periodâ€”was about 6.0 before the Great Leap
Forward, declined to 3.3 in 1961, rose to 7.5 in 1963, returned to 6.0 in the
mid-1960s, fell steeply to only 2.2 in 1980, and then rose slightly to over 2.6 in
1981 and 1982.

text: The birth data on which these fertility rates are based are derived from the new detailed information, especially that from the fertility survey.
text_raw:
The birth data on which these fertility rates are based are
derived from the new detailed information, especially that from the fertility
survey.

text: It is clear that the number of births previously listed in official sources has been incomplete: by more than 15 percent in the 1950s, by less than 10 percent in the late 1960s and early 1970s, and by 15 percent or more since the intensification of the antinatalist program in 1979.
text_raw:
It is clear that the number of births previously listed in official sources
has been incomplete: by more than 15 percent in the 1950s, by less than 10
percent in the late 1960s and early 1970s, and by 15 percent or more since the
intensification of the antinatalist program in 1979.

text: Age Pattern of Fertility.
text_raw: Age Pattern of Fertility.

text: The age pattern of fertility of married women in the 1950s was a pattern of gradual decline in the rate of childbearing with age until age 30; the decline steepened after age 30 and especially after age 35.
text_raw:
The age pattern of fertility of married women in
the 1950s was a pattern of gradual decline in the rate of childbearing with age
until age 30; the decline steepened after age 30 and especially after age 35.

text: This age pattern closely resembles the early gradual and later steep decline of marital fertility rates with age of woman that is characteristic of populations in which couples practice little contraception or induced abortion.
text_raw:
This
age pattern closely resembles the early gradual and later steep decline of marital
fertility rates with age of woman that is characteristic of populations in which
couples practice little contraception or induced abortion.

text: This age pattern of marital fertility in the 1950s supports the inference of little use of contraception.
text_raw:
This age pattern of
marital fertility in the 1950s supports the inference of little use of contraception.

text: In the 1970s (and especially in 1980), by contrast, marital fertility rates fell very steeply with age of women after their late 20s, a pattern characteristic of very general resort to contraception to limit fertility after desired family size is reached.
text_raw:

steeply with age of women after their late 20s, a pattern characteristic of very

reached.

text: Introduction SCOPE OF THE REPORT This report is a summary of fertility, nuptiality, and mortality in the People's Republic of China from the early 1950s to 1982.
text_raw:
Introduction
SCOPE OF THE REPORT
This report is a summary of fertility, nuptiality, and mortality in the
People's Republic of China from the early 1950s to 1982.

text: It is based largely on the single-year age distributions tabulated in the censuses of 1953, 1964, and 1982 (with some adjustment) and the detailed history of fertility and nuptiality collected in the large-scale 1982 survey of retrospective experience among 311,000 women aged 15-67.
text_raw:
It is based largely on
the single-year age distributions tabulated in the censuses of 1953, 1964, and
1982 (with some adjustment) and the detailed history of fertility and nuptiality
collected in the large-scale 1982 survey of retrospective experience among
311,000 women aged 15-67.

text: The survey was conducted by the State Family Planning Commission.
text_raw:
The survey was conducted by the State Family
Planning Commission.

text: Much of the data presented here are taken from a special issue of the Chinese journal Population and Economics, published in 1983, which was devoted to detailed information about the fertility survey and its results.

Chinese journal

text: In most censuses the reported age distribution is distorted by what demographers call age-heaping, a tendency for too many persons to be reported at ages that respondents favor (usually ages ending in 0 or 5).
text_raw:
In most
censuses the reported age distribution is distorted by what demographers call

respondents favor (usually ages ending in 0 or 5).

text: However, because most intercensal intervals are either 5 or 10 years, the effect of age-heaping on survival ratios is usually dampened because preferred ages (e.g., 30 and 40) are in both numerator and denominator of the ratios.
text_raw:
However, because most
intercensal intervals are either 5 or 10 years, the effect of age-heaping on
survival ratios is usually dampened because preferred ages (e.g., 30 and 40) are
in both numerator and denominator of the ratios.

text: In China the intercensal intervals are 11 years and 18 years, but the survival ratios show almost no effect of age-heaping: from 1953 to 1964 the survival ratios for women aged 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, and 60 in 1953 are slightly too low (a favored age is in the denominator) and ratios at 29, 39, and 49 are slightly too high (a favored age is in the numerator), but the effect is very small.
text_raw:

text: The high survival ratio from age 0 in 1953 to age 11 in 1964 is almost certainly the result of an undercount of infants under age 1 in 1953, possibly caused by age misstatement that inflates the number at age 1, leading to too low a survival ratio for this cohort.

text: That very accurate information about age can be obtained from a Chinese population is well known.
text_raw:
That
very accurate information about age can be obtained from a Chinese population

text: The reason is a cultural one.
text_raw: The reason is a cultural one.

text: People of East Asian culture (Chinese, Japanese, Korean, etc.) almost universally know their date of birth, even when illiterate, usually in terms of the animal year of birth (in a cycle of 12 animals and 5 different qualities for each animal, a complete cycle that repeats every 60 years) and the lunar month.
text_raw:
People of East Asian culture
(Chinese, Japanese, Korean, etc.) almost universally know their date of birth,
even when illiterate, usually in terms of the animal year of birth (in a cycle of
12 animals and 5 different qualities for each animal, a complete cycle that
repeats every 60 years) and the lunar month.

text: Because of this knowledge, if age is determined through a question asking the date of birth, followed by use of a formula that converts the animal year and lunar month to a Western date, age can be determined with precision.
text_raw:
Because of this knowledge, if age
is determined through a question asking the date of birth, followed by use of a
formula that converts the animal year and lunar month to a Western date, age
can be determined with precision.

text: Conclusions The welcome flood of accurate demographic data from China provides an unusually detailed depiction of an extraordinary population.
text_raw:
Conclusions
The welcome flood of accurate demographic data from China provides an
unusually detailed depiction of an extraordinary population.

text: Being the most populous nation in the world has not prevented the People's Republic of China from compressing into a short time very big reductions in fertility (more than 50 percent in a decade) and mortality (more than 20 years added to the expectation of life at birth in about 15 years).
text_raw:
Being the most
populous nation in the world has not prevented the People's Republic of China
from compressing into a short time very big reductions in fertility (more than 50
percent in a decade) and mortality (more than 20 years added to the expectation
of life at birth in about 15 years).

text: The earliest data are not inconsistent with the fertility (about the same TFR) and nuptiality (marriage about 1 year later) of traditional China, as reconstructed from a survey around 1930.
text_raw:
The earliest data are not inconsistent with the
fertility (about the same TFR) and nuptiality (marriage about 1 year later) of
traditional China, as reconstructed from a survey around 1930.

text: The latest data are not inconsistent with some of the principal demographic characteristics of developed countries two or three decades ago.
text_raw:
The latest data
are not inconsistent with some of the principal demographic characteristics of
developed countries two or three decades ago.

text: The most recent TFR in China is about the same as in the United States or a typical population in Western Europe in the 1960s; the recent average duration of life is not far from that attained in those populations about 30 years ago.
text_raw:
The most recent TFR in China is
about the same as in the United States or a typical population in Western
Europe in the 1960s; the recent average duration of life is not far from that
attained in those populations about 30 years ago.

text: Age at marriage has also changed from the very early norms traditional in much of Asia to ages more like those found in the West.
text_raw:
Age at marriage has also
changed from the very early norms traditional in much of Asia to ages more like
those found in the West.

text: The rapid changes of fertility, mortality, and nuptiality in China have not been without costs (the excess mortality and abnormal reduction with subsequent abnormal recovery in fertility in the "bitter years").
text_raw:
The rapid changes of fertility, mortality, and nuptiality in China have not
been without costs (the excess mortality and abnormal reduction with
subsequent abnormal recovery in fertility in the "bitter years").

text: That the surprisingly rapid changes have also incurred grave social costs can be inferred from the recent decision to reduce pressure for late marriage and from the anomalous high male/female ratio of births of second and higher order in 1981.
text_raw:
That the
surprisingly rapid changes have also incurred grave social costs can be inferred
from the recent decision to reduce pressure for late marriage and from the
anomalous high male/female ratio of births of second and higher order in 1981.

text: The marriage boom of 1981-82 is not the only obstacle to attaining and maintaining very low fertility.
text_raw:
The marriage boom of 1981-82 is not the only obstacle to attaining and
maintaining very low fertility.

text: The life tables are constructed by an extension of a method devised by Preston and Coale (1982).

text: In brief, the construction involves calculating the number of persons who cross each exact age x in the intercensal period, an estimate derived by interpolation between the number enumerated in each cohort in the earlier and later censuses.
text_raw:

number of persons who cross each exact age x in the intercensal period, an
estimate derived by interpolation between the number enumerated in each
cohort in the earlier and later censuses.

text: When the data are accurate, the method yields a life table that is an exact expression of intercensal mortality by age.
text_raw:

yields a life table that is an exact expression of intercensal mortality by age.

text: A full description of the method is contained in Coale (1984).
text_raw:

full description of the method is contained in Coale (1984).

text: A more precise estimate can be obtained for each single year of age by allowing for the fact that the proportion surviving from one age to another is not an exactly linear sequence.

text: More appropriate, slightly nonlinear interpolation is achieved by deriving interpolation factors from a model life table at about the right level of mortality.

text: The births derived from the age-specific fertility rates are for calendar years (January 1 to December 31); the births compatible with the census age distributions are for ''fiscal'' years (July 1 to June 30) because the censuses were taken as of midyear.
